analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate lower drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices was introduced by Sen. Al Franken in January 2011, never gained a single cosponsor, and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law blocks the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering in drug price negotiations or setting a price structure for Medicare's prescription drug benefit, and denies the Secretary the negotiating power that other federal agencies already have. This bill would repeal that prohibition and direct the Secretary to negotiate contracts with drug manufacturers to get the lowest possible prices for Medicare beneficiaries. It also required twice-yearly reports to Congress on how the negotiations were lowering prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare's roughly 47 million beneficiaries, who pay out-of-pocket costs tied to drug prices, and by extension taxpayers who fund Medicare Part D through premiums and general revenue. Any lowering of drug prices seniors pay at the pharmacy reduces their cost burden.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the 'noninterference' clause of the Medicare Part D statute, which forbids HHS from interfering in negotiations between drug makers and plan sponsors and from setting a reimbursement price structure [S2][S3].

It grants the Secretary of HHS 'authority similar to that of other Federal entities that purchase prescription drugs in bulk to negotiate contracts with manufacturers' of covered Part D drugs, with the stated goal that beneficiaries 'pay the lowest possible price' [S3].
It requires the Secretary to report to Congress every six months, starting one year after enactment, describing how the negotiations are achieving lower prices for beneficiaries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Medicare Part D sales are currently made at prices the government is barred by statute from negotiating. If the Secretary negotiated lower prices, the cost would come out of manufacturer revenues.

drawbacks.text: The bill as written gives the Secretary broad negotiating authority without specifying how negotiated prices would be structured or enforced, which supporters of the existing Part D design argued could evolve into government-set price controls and reduce drug companies' returns on investment, potentially affecting development incentives over time.

The bill would have changed the system under which private plans currently negotiate on behalf of Part D beneficiaries; critics of government negotiation contend that plan-sponsor bargaining and formulary competition already produce discounts, so the budget savings and price reductions were uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct: the government is the largest buyer of prescription drugs in the country, and giving it the same bargaining power other federal buyers already have is a straightforward way to lower prices seniors pay. The main honest objection is design, not principle — the bill leaves the mechanics of negotiation to the Secretary rather than writing price standards into law, and the size of any savings was untested. The bill's fatal problem was not its design but its support: it drew no cosponsors and never received a committee hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and that is where it stayed — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, until the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Al Franken introduced S. 31 on January 25, 2011, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action of any kind appears in the record for the remainder of the 112th Congress; the bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the statutory 'noninterference' clause barring Medicare from negotiating prices remained in force for the rest of the 112th Congress, so Part D prices continued to be set without government bargaining power.

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke to its referral in floor remarks; the bill's only Senate supporter of record.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the full two-year Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry with a direct financial stake in preserving the Part D noninterference clause
against.what_they_did: Defended the existing law that bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices, which the bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other senator of either party signed on, so the partisan shape is unknown; the bill drew zero cosponsors from both parties [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the statute that bars HHS from negotiating Part D drug prices, opening the largest drug market in the country to government bargaining. Lower negotiated prices would come directly out of manufacturer revenue, so the industry's interest in keeping the noninterference clause runs against seniors who pay Part D drug costs.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: Today private plan sponsors and their PBMs are the sole negotiators with drug makers; the bill would have added a second, public negotiator alongside them. Their negotiating role would not disappear, but the bill's stated goal was to get beneficiaries 'the lowest possible price', which could compress the margins PBMs earn on Part D spreads.
